titleFa: کتاب Modern Man in Search of a Soul
titleEn: Modern Man in Search of a Soul
author: Carl Gustav Jung
introFa: کتاب «Modern Man in Search of a Soul» نوشته Carl Gustav Jung یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Modern Man in Search of a Soul»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Book reviews 443 non-proven, but probably unfavourable, with a plea for non-clinical studies to counteract the epistemic defects in the psychoanalytical method. Most of these defects are illustrated by Heinz Kohut's brave but unconvincing attempt to defend his credo by reference to its still unsubstantiated efficacy as a mode of treatment. Modern Man in Search of a Soul. By C. G. Jung. (Pp. 282; £3.95.) Answer to Job. By C. G. Jung. (Pp. 194; £3.95.) Both from Ark Paperbacks/Routledge & Kegan Paul: London. 1984. This pair of paperback imprints reveals the two faces of Carl Jung. The first volume, originally published in 1933 and since reprinted many times, contains eleven chapters based on lectures, most of them down-to-earth accounts of his outlook on psychotherapy and cognate clinical issues. However, in the last three papers - "The Basic Postulates of Analytical Psychology',' The Spiritual Problem of Modern Man' and' Psycho- therapists or the Clergy'-another theme emerges:' patients force the psychotherapist into the role of a priest... That is why we psychothera- pists must occupy ourselves with problems which, strictly speaking, belong to the theolo- gian'. In his Answer to Job, written twenty years later, Jung has discarded his white coat to don sacerdotal robes. His concerns are openly theological; he is not even certain whether' God and the unconscious are two different entities.' Either way, for believers he remains a guide and mentor; for agnostics, there is more than a hint of flim-flammery. Fanaticism. By A. Haynal, M. Molnar and G. de Puymege. (Pp. 282; $19.95.) Schocken Books: New York. 1983. Hitler's Psychopathology. By N. Bromberg and V. V. Small. (Pp. 335; $27.50.) International Universities Press: New York. 1984. Psychohistory a la frangaise is well illustrated by the first of these two books, a passable translation of Le Fanatisme: ses racines; Un essai historique et psychanalytique. The concept of the fanatic and his/her credo is ill-defined but sufficiently well-recognized to enable the three authors, two historians and a psychoanalyst at the University of Geneva, to produce a triune 15 essay composed of variegated chapters on such topics as etymology, sectarianism, anti-Semitism, chauvinism and, inevitably, the French Revolu- tion, followed by a rambling discussion between themselves. The text is filled with evidence of wide reading, historical anecdotes and cloudy generalizations, all permeated with out-dated psychoanalytical speculation. The inclusion of a postscript to the American edition points to a potential transatlantic readership, presumably the one for which Bromberg & Small have written their piece of psychohistory a I'ameri- caine, an altogether cruder variety than its French counterpart. It consists in a garish account of Hitler's life, cobbled together from several sources, presented with plenty of psycho- dynamics as an example of the career of a 'narcissistic-borderline personality disorder'. The judges at Nuremberg saw things differently. Visionary Vine. By M. Dobkin de Rios. (Pp. 161; illustrated; price not stated.) Waveland Press: Illinois. 1984. This reprint of a monograph by an American anthropologist was first published in 1972. In it the author gives an account of her field-work devoted to folk-psychotherapy and the ritual use of the hallucinogenic drug, ayahuasca, among inhabitants of the city of Iquitos on the Amazon river in Peru. Like many studies by participant observers, the exotic material is colourfully presented but essentially anecdotal and of descriptive rather than scientific value. The phenomena may well be authentic but the interpretation placed upon them, and especially on the mechanisms of healing, is largely speculative. Conditions of Happiness. By R. Veenhoven. (Pp.470; illustrated; $56.00.) D. Reidel: Dordrecht. 1984. Although deemed important enough to merit inclusion in the American Declaration of Independence, happiness has proved to be a curiously elusive concept. Now, it seems, the heavy hands of the sociologists are being put to the plough. This book, written by a Dutch sociologist, is derived from the material contained in 245 empirical studies concerned with 'valid indices' of happiness. A companion volume PSM 15
